claim: The basal forebrain (BF) plays key roles in sleep-wake regulation, attention, and learning/memory.
source: The basal forebrain (BF) plays key roles in multiple brain functions, including sleep-wake regulation, attention, and learning/memory, but the long-range connections mediating these functions remain poorly characterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific literature on BF functions.

claim: The long-range connections of the basal forebrain mediating its functions remain poorly characterized.
source: The basal forebrain (BF) plays key roles in multiple brain functions, including sleep-wake regulation, attention, and learning/memory, but the long-range connections mediating these functions remain poorly characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Four BF cell types were mapped: cholinergic, glutamatergic, parvalbumin-positive (PV+) GABAergic, and somatostatin-positive (SOM+) GABAergic neurons.
source: Here we performed whole-brain mapping of both inputs and outputs of four BF cell types – cholinergic, glutamatergic, and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and somatostatin-positive (SOM+) GABAergic neurons – in the mouse brain.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and cell types studied.

claim: Rabies virus-mediated monosynaptic retrograde tracing was used to label inputs to BF cell types.
source: Using rabies virus -mediated monosynaptic retrograde tracing to label the inputs and adeno-associated virus to trace axonal projections, we identified numerous brain areas connected to the BF.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for input tracing.

claim: Adeno-associated virus was used to trace axonal projections from BF cell types.
source: Using rabies virus -mediated monosynaptic retrograde tracing to label the inputs and adeno-associated virus to trace axonal projections, we identified numerous brain areas connected to the BF.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for output tracing.

claim: Numerous brain areas are connected to the BF.
source: Using rabies virus -mediated monosynaptic retrograde tracing to label the inputs and adeno-associated virus to trace axonal projections, we identified numerous brain areas connected to the BF.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The inputs to different BF cell types were qualitatively similar.
source: The inputs to different cell types were qualitatively similar, but the output projections showed marked differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing input distributions across cell types.

claim: The output projections from different BF cell types showed marked differences.
source: The inputs to different cell types were qualitatively similar, but the output projections showed marked differences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing output distributions across cell types.

claim: The connections to glutamatergic and SOM+ neurons were strongly reciprocal.
source: The connections to glutamatergic and SOM+ neurons were strongly reciprocal, while those to cholinergic and PV+ neurons were more unidirectional.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing input and output distributions for these cell types.

claim: The connections to cholinergic and PV+ neurons were more unidirectional.
source: The connections to glutamatergic and SOM+ neurons were strongly reciprocal, while those to cholinergic and PV+ neurons were more unidirectional.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing input and output distributions for these cell types.

claim: The BF circuit has highly convergent inputs and divergent outputs.
source: These results reveal the long-range wiring diagram of the BF circuit with highly convergent inputs and divergent outputs and point to both functional commonality and specialization of different BF cell types.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the input and output mapping data.

claim: Different BF cell types show both functional commonality and specialization.
source: These results reveal the long-range wiring diagram of the BF circuit with highly convergent inputs and divergent outputs and point to both functional commonality and specialization of different BF cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of inputs and differences in outputs across cell types.

claim: The BF has been implicated in arousal, attention, and plasticity.
source: The BF has been implicated in a variety of brain functions such as arousal, attention, and plasticity (Bakin and Weinberger, 1996; Brown et al., 2012; Everitt and Robbins, 1997; Froemke et al., 2013; Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Jones, 2011; Lin et al., 2015; Saper et al., 2010; Sarter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysfunction or loss of BF cholinergic neurons is an important feature of Alzheimer's disease associated with cognitive impairment.
source: The dysfunction or loss of BF cholinergic neurons is an important feature of Alzheimer's disease associated with cognitive impairment (Schliebs and Arendt, 2011; Whitehouse et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Alzheimer's disease.

claim: BF neurons form extensive local synapses.
source: In addition to forming extensive local synapses (Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014; Zaborszky and Duque, 2000), BF neurons receive inputs (Asanuma, 1989; Freund and Meskenaite, 1992; Grove, 1988a, Henny and Jones, 2006; Manns et al., 2001; Parent et al., 1988; Rye et al., 1984; Semba et al., 1988; Zaborszky and Cullinan, 1992) and send outputs (Cullinan and Zaborszky, 1991; Grove, 1988b; Jones and Cuello, 1989; Mesulam and Mufson, 1984; Paré and Smith, 1994) to many other brain areas (Steriade and McCarley, 2005; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BF neurons receive inputs from many brain areas.
source: In addition to forming extensive local synapses (Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014; Zaborszky and Duque, 2000), BF neurons receive inputs (Asanuma, 1989; Freund and Meskenaite, 1992; Grove, 1988a, Henny and Jones, 2006; Manns et al., 2001; Parent et al., 1988; Rye et al., 1984; Semba et al., 1988; Zaborszky and Cullinan, 1992) and send outputs (Cullinan and Zaborszky, 1991; Grove, 1988b; Jones and Cuello, 1989; Mesulam and Mufson, 1984; Paré and Smith, 1994) to many other brain areas (Steriade and McCarley, 2005; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BF neurons send outputs to many brain areas.
source: In addition to forming extensive local synapses (Xu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014; Zaborszky and Duque, 2000), BF neurons receive inputs (Asanuma, 1989; Freund and Meskenaite, 1992; Grove, 1988a, Henny and Jones, 2006; Manns et al., 2001; Parent et al., 1988; Rye et al., 1984; Semba et al., 1988; Zaborszky and Cullinan, 1992) and send outputs (Cullinan and Zaborszky, 1991; Grove, 1988b; Jones and Cuello, 1989; Mesulam and Mufson, 1984; Paré and Smith, 1994) to many other brain areas (Steriade and McCarley, 2005; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are three major cell types spatially intermingled in the BF: cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic.
source: There are three major cell types spatially intermingled in the BF: cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic (Semba, 2000; Zaborszky et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 192-IgG-saporin-mediated lesion of cholinergic neurons impaired the ability of rats to discriminate between signal and non-signal visual events in an attention task.
source: For example, 192-IgG-saporin-mediated lesion of cholinergic neurons impaired the ability of rats to discriminate between signal and non-signal visual events in an attention task (McGaughy et al., 1996) and disrupted training-induced cortical map reorganization associated with motor learning (Conner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 192-IgG-saporin-mediated lesion of cholinergic neurons disrupted training-induced cortical map reorganization associated with motor learning.
source: For example, 192-IgG-saporin-mediated lesion of cholinergic neurons impaired the ability of rats to discriminate between signal and non-signal visual events in an attention task (McGaughy et al., 1996) and disrupted training-induced cortical map reorganization associated with motor learning (Conner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The activity of non-cholinergic BF neurons correlates with sustained attention.
source: For example, in recent studies the activity of non-cholinergic BF neurons was found to correlate with sustained attention (Hangya et al., 2015) or to encode reward and motivational salience information (Avila and Lin, 2014; Lin and Nicolelis, 2008; Nguyen and Lin, 2014), and optogenetic activation of PV+ GABAergic neurons was shown to regulate cortical gamma oscillations (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Non-cholinergic BF neurons encode reward and motivational salience information.
source: For example, in recent studies the activity of non-cholinergic BF neurons was found to correlate with sustained attention (Hangya et al., 2015) or to encode reward and motivational salience information (Avila and Lin, 2014; Lin and Nicolelis, 2008; Nguyen and Lin, 2014), and optogenetic activation of PV+ GABAergic neurons was shown to regulate cortical gamma oscillations (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PV+ GABAergic neurons regulates cortical gamma oscillations.
source: For example, in recent studies the activity of non-cholinergic BF neurons was found to correlate with sustained attention (Hangya et al., 2015) or to encode reward and motivational salience information (Avila and Lin, 2014; Lin and Nicolelis, 2008; Nguyen and Lin, 2014), and optogenetic activation of PV+ GABAergic neurons was shown to regulate cortical gamma oscillations (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cholinergic, glutamatergic, and PV+ neuron activity promotes wakefulness.
source: In a study on sleep-wake control, cholinergic, glutamatergic, and PV+ neuron activity was found to promote wakefulness, while SOM+ neurons promoted sleep; these four cell types form extensive but highly specific local connections with each other for brain-state regulation (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SOM+ neurons promote sleep.
source: In a study on sleep-wake control, cholinergic, glutamatergic, and PV+ neuron activity was found to promote wakefulness, while SOM+ neurons promoted sleep; these four cell types form extensive but highly specific local connections with each other for brain-state regulation (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The four BF cell types form extensive but highly specific local connections with each other for brain-state regulation.
source: In a study on sleep-wake control, cholinergic, glutamatergic, and PV+ neuron activity was found to promote wakefulness, while SOM+ neurons promoted sleep; these four cell types form extensive but highly specific local connections with each other for brain-state regulation (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ChAT-Cre, VGLUT2-Cre, PV-Cre, and SOM-Cre mouse lines label largely non-overlapping BF neuron populations with high specificity.
source: These four Cre lines have been shown to label largely non-overlapping BF neuron populations with high specificity (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RV-mediated transsynaptic retrograde tracing labels monosynaptic inputs to selected starter cells with high specificity.
source: To identify the long-range inputs to each cell type, we used RV-mediated transsynaptic retrograde tracing, which has been shown to label monosynaptic inputs to selected starter cells with high specificity (Miyamichi et al., 2011; Wall et al., 2013; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012; Wickersham et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on the method.

claim: The expression of RG was highly cell type specific and not detected in wild-type mice not expressing Cre recombinase.
source: The expression of RG was highly cell type specific and not detected in wild-type mice not expressing Cre recombinase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 900 – 14,631 (median 7002) tdTomato-labeled presynaptic neurons were found in each brain (n = 17).
source: We found 900 – 14,631 (median 7002) tdTomato-labeled presynaptic neurons in each brain (n = 17), and the convergence index (ratio between the number of input cells and starter cells) ranged between 4.3 and 77.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the input tracing experiments.

claim: The convergence index (ratio between the number of input cells and starter cells) ranged between 4.3 and 77.7.
source: We found 900 – 14,631 (median 7002) tdTomato-labeled presynaptic neurons in each brain (n = 17), and the convergence index (ratio between the number of input cells and starter cells) ranged between 4.3 and 77.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the input tracing experiments.

claim: The presynaptic neurons were predominantly ipsilateral to the starter population (<5% contralateral).
source: The presynaptic neurons were predominantly ipsilateral to the starter population (<5% contralateral) but were distributed in a large number of brain areas (Figure 2, Figure 3, Video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the input tracing data.

claim: The striatum and hypothalamus provided the highest numbers of inputs to BF neurons.
source: When the brain was divided into 12 major regions (Figure 3A), the striatum and hypothalamus provided the highest numbers of inputs, while few labeled neurons were found in the medulla or cerebellum (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative analysis of input distributions in Figure 3A.

claim: Few labeled input neurons were found in the medulla or cerebellum.
source: When the brain was divided into 12 major regions (Figure 3A), the striatum and hypothalamus provided the highest numbers of inputs, while few labeled neurons were found in the medulla or cerebellum (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative analysis of input distributions in Figure 3A.

claim: The nucleus accumbens, lateral hypothalamus, and central nucleus of the amygdala were among the structures containing the highest numbers of input neurons.
source: When the input distribution was analyzed at a finer spatial scale (e.g., the 6th ring of the sunburst plot), the nucleus accumbens (Mesulam and Mufson, 1984; Zaborszky and Cullinan, 1992), lateral hypothalamus (Cullinan and Zaborszky, 1991; Grove, 1988b; Mesulam and Mufson, 1984), and central nucleus of the amygdala (Grove, 1988b; Pare and Smith, 1994) were among the structures containing the highest numbers of input neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons received significantly more inputs from the lateral hypothalamus than the other cell types.
source: For example, glutamatergic neurons received significantly more inputs from the lateral hypothalamus than the other cell types (P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. ChAT; P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. PV; P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. SOM;, one-way ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey's test), and PV+ neurons received more inputs from the nucleus accumbens (ACB) (P = 0.004, PV vs. ChAT; P = 0.003, PV vs. VGLUT2; P = 0.001, PV vs. SOM; one-way ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey's test).
evidence: This is a statistically significant finding from quantitative comparison of input distributions.

claim: PV+ neurons received more inputs from the nucleus accumbens than the other cell types.
source: For example, glutamatergic neurons received significantly more inputs from the lateral hypothalamus than the other cell types (P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. ChAT; P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. PV; P = 0.001, VGLUT2 vs. SOM;, one-way ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey's test), and PV+ neurons received more inputs from the nucleus accumbens (ACB) (P = 0.004, PV vs. ChAT; P = 0.003, PV vs. VGLUT2; P = 0.001, PV vs. SOM; one-way ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey's test).
evidence: This is a statistically significant finding from quantitative comparison of input distributions.

claim: Activating ChR2-expressing prefrontal cortex axon terminals with blue light evoked excitatory responses in all recorded BF cholinergic neurons (n = 9).
source: Activating the ChR2-expressing axon terminals with blue light evoked excitatory responses in all recorded BF cholinergic neurons (n = 9, Figure 4B and C), confirming the input revealed with RV tracing.
evidence: This is an electrophysiological validation of the anatomical tracing results.

claim: All four BF cell types received inhibitory responses from the ACB.
source: We found that all four BF cell types received inhibitory responses from the ACB (Figure 4D and E; ChAT+: 2 out 5 showed significant responses; VGLUT2+: 2/4; PV+: 3/3; SOM+: 4/8), which is consistent with the finding of an electron microscopic double-immunolabeling study performed in rats (Zaborszky and Cullinan, 1992).
evidence: This is an electrophysiological finding that validates the anatomical tracing and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Each BF cell type projected to a large number of brain areas (>95% ipsilateral).
source: Parallel to the broad distribution of inputs (Figure 3), we found that each BF cell type also projected to a large number of brain areas (Figure 5, Figure 6, Video 2, http://sleepcircuits.org/bf/, >95% ipsilateral).
evidence: This is a finding from the output tracing experiments.

claim: Among the 12 major brain subdivisions, the hypothalamus, pallidum, and striatum received the heaviest BF projections.
source: Among the 12 major brain subdivisions (Figure 6A), the hypothalamus, pallidum, and striatum received the heaviest BF projections (Grove, 1988a; Henny and Jones, 2006), while very few axons were detected in the medulla or cerebellum (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Very few BF axons were detected in the medulla or cerebellum.
source: Among the 12 major brain subdivisions (Figure 6A), the hypothalamus, pallidum, and striatum received the heaviest BF projections (Grove, 1988a; Henny and Jones, 2006), while very few axons were detected in the medulla or cerebellum (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lateral hypothalamus was a major recipient of BF projections.
source: In addition to providing extensive inputs to the BF (Figure 2), the lateral hypothalamus was also a major recipient of BF projections (Figure 5), indicating a strong BF-hypothalamus loop that may be important for brain-state regulation (Brown et al., 2012; Jones, 2011; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and the inference about the BF-hypothalamus loop is supported by citations.

claim: There is a strong BF-hypothalamus loop that may be important for brain-state regulation.
source: In addition to providing extensive inputs to the BF (Figure 2), the lateral hypothalamus was also a major recipient of BF projections (Figure 5), indicating a strong BF-hypothalamus loop that may be important for brain-state regulation (Brown et al., 2012; Jones, 2011; Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal connectivity data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Compared to the other cell types, the projection from cholinergic neurons was much stronger in the basolateral amygdala, hippocampus, and visual cortex but much weaker in the lateral hypothalamus, lateral habenula, and the ventral tegmental area.
source: For example, compared to the other cell types, the projection from cholinergic neurons was much stronger in the basolateral amygdala, hippocampus, and visual cortex but much weaker in the lateral hypothalamus, lateral habenula, and the ventral tegmental area (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 comparing output patterns across cell types.

claim: For input distribution, the correlation coefficients between all cell types were high.
source: For input distribution, the CCs between all cell types were high (Figure 7A), confirming their overall similarity observed earlier (Figure 2, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Higher correlation coefficients were found between samples of the same cell type (0.81 ± 0.04) than of different cell types (0.70 ± 0.02, P = 0.01) for input distributions.
source: On the other hand, when we computed the CCs between individual brain samples, we found higher CCs between samples of the same cell type (0.81 ± 0.04, s.e.m.) than of different cell types (0.70 ± 0.02, P = 0.01, t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statistically significant finding from quantitative analysis.

claim: Despite overall similarity, there were genuine differences in input distributions between cell types that were beyond experimental variability.
source: This indicates that despite the overall similarity, there were genuine differences between cell types that were beyond experimental variability.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: The correlation coefficients between individual samples of the same cell type were high (0.86 ± 0.05) for output distribution.
source: For output distribution, the CCs between individual samples of the same cell type were also high (0.86 ± 0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), indicating reproducibility of the mapping.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of experimental reproducibility.

claim: Most of the correlation coefficients between cell types for output distribution were much lower than those for input distribution.
source: However, most of the CCs between cell types (Figure 7B, computed after averaging across samples of the same cell type) were much lower than those for input distribution.
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Cholinergic neurons project strongly to structures within the cerebral cortex and weakly to the brain stem structures.
source: The two lowest CCs (ChAT+ vs. VGLUT2+ and PV+ neurons) reflect the fact that while the cholinergic neurons project strongly to structures within the cerebral cortex (including olfactory areas, isocortex, hippocampus, and cortical subplate) and weakly to the brain stem structures (thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain), glutamatergic and PV+ neurons (with output distributions highly similar to each other) showed complementary projection patterns (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and explains the low correlation coefficients.

claim: Glutamatergic and PV+ neurons showed complementary projection patterns to cholinergic neurons.
source: The two lowest CCs (ChAT+ vs. VGLUT2+ and PV+ neurons) reflect the fact that while the cholinergic neurons project strongly to structures within the cerebral cortex (including olfactory areas, isocortex, hippocampus, and cortical subplate) and weakly to the brain stem structures (thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain), glutamatergic and PV+ neurons (with output distributions highly similar to each other) showed complementary projection patterns (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and explains the low correlation coefficients.

claim: The highest correlation coefficient between input and output distributions was found for SOM+ neurons.
source: Finally, we computed the CC between the input and output distributions of each cell type (Figure 7C). The highest CC was found for SOM+ neurons, reflecting their strong reciprocal connections with a number of brain structures, including the hypothalamus, striatum, pallidum, and olfactory areas (Figure 7D, lower right, Figure 7—source data 1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and explained by the reciprocal connectivity pattern.

claim: SOM+ neurons have strong reciprocal connections with the hypothalamus, striatum, pallidum, and olfactory areas.
source: The highest CC was found for SOM+ neurons, reflecting their strong reciprocal connections with a number of brain structures, including the hypothalamus, striatum, pallidum, and olfactory areas (Figure 7D, lower right, Figure 7—source data 1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons have strong reciprocal connections with the hypothalamus and striatum.
source: For glutamatergic neurons, the high CC reflects their strong reciprocal connections with the hypothalamus and striatum (Figure 7D, upper right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: For cholinergic and PV+ GABAergic neurons, the correlation coefficients between input and output distributions were much lower.
source: For cholinergic and PV+ GABAergic neurons, the CCs between input and output distributions were much lower, reflecting the facts that while both cell types receive strong input from the striatum, cholinergic neurons project strongly to the cerebral cortex, and PV+ neurons to the pallidum and hypothalamus (Figure 7D, upper and lower left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and explained by the non-reciprocal connectivity patterns shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both cholinergic and PV+ neurons receive strong input from the striatum.
source: For cholinergic and PV+ GABAergic neurons, the CCs between input and output distributions were much lower, reflecting the facts that while both cell types receive strong input from the striatum, cholinergic neurons project strongly to the cerebral cortex, and PV+ neurons to the pallidum and hypothalamus (Figure 7D, upper and lower left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cholinergic neurons project strongly to the cerebral cortex.
source: For cholinergic and PV+ GABAergic neurons, the CCs between input and output distributions were much lower, reflecting the facts that while both cell types receive strong input from the striatum, cholinergic neurons project strongly to the cerebral cortex, and PV+ neurons to the pallidum and hypothalamus (Figure 7D, upper and lower left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: PV+ neurons project strongly to the pallidum and hypothalamus.
source: For cholinergic and PV+ GABAergic neurons, the CCs between input and output distributions were much lower, reflecting the facts that while both cell types receive strong input from the striatum, cholinergic neurons project strongly to the cerebral cortex, and PV+ neurons to the pallidum and hypothalamus (Figure 7D, upper and lower left).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cortical inputs to all four BF cell types originate primarily from the agranular insular and orbital areas of the prefrontal cortex.
source: For example, we found that cortical inputs (Mesulam and Mufson, 1984; Steriade and McCarley, 2005) to all four BF cell types originate primarily from the agranular insular and orbital areas of the prefrontal cortex (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RV-mediated transsynaptic tracing demonstrated extensive monosynaptic innervation from prefrontal cortex to BF cholinergic neurons.
source: While a previous ultrastructural study failed to detect convincing synaptic contact between prefrontal axons and BF cholinergic neurons (Zaborszky et al., 1997), our RV-mediated transsynaptic tracing demonstrated extensive monosynaptic innervation, which was also validated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the RV tracing data and validated by electrophysiology.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the BF are strongly activated by reinforcement signals during an auditory detection task.
source: A recent study showed that cholinergic neurons in the BF are strongly activated by reinforcement signals during an auditory detection task (Hangya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The whole-brain mapping of BF cholinergic neuron inputs provides a list of candidate neurons through which reinforcement signals are conveyed to the BF cholinergic neurons.
source: Our whole-brain mapping of their inputs provides a list of candidate neurons through which the reinforcement signals are conveyed to the BF cholinergic neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the input mapping data in the context of prior findings.

claim: The distinct projection patterns between cholinergic and glutamatergic/PV+ neurons suggest that they preferentially regulate different brain functions during wakeful states.
source: The distinct projection patterns between cholinergic and glutamatergic/PV+ neurons (Figure 6) suggest that they preferentially regulate different brain functions during wakeful states.
evidence: This is inferred from the output mapping data in the context of prior findings about their roles in wakefulness.

claim: PV+ neurons have extensive subcortical projections that may contribute to the regulation of cortical gamma oscillations.
source: In addition to direct projections to the cortex, our study showed extensive subcortical projections of PV neurons, which may also contribute to the regulation of cortical gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is inferred from the output mapping data in the context of prior findings about PV neurons and gamma oscillations.

claim: The broad GABAergic inhibition of input areas by SOM+ neurons may be important for the sleep-promoting effect.
source: The output distribution of SOM+ neurons, on the other hand, was highly correlated with the input distributions of all BF cell types (Figure 7C, bottom row); the broad GABAergic inhibition of these input areas by SOM+ neurons may be important for the sleep-promoting effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the output mapping data in the context of prior findings about SOM+ neurons and sleep.

claim: The highly convergent inputs from multiple brain areas allow a variety of sensory, motor, cognitive, and emotional signals to be integrated within the BF.
source: Thus, while the highly convergent inputs from multiple brain areas allow a variety of sensory, motor, cognitive, and emotional signals to be integrated within the BF, the distinct projections by different cell types may enhance the versatility of the BF in coordinating diverse functions of multiple brain networks.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad input distributions observed across cell types.

claim: The distinct projections by different cell types may enhance the versatility of the BF in coordinating diverse functions of multiple brain networks.
source: Thus, while the highly convergent inputs from multiple brain areas allow a variety of sensory, motor, cognitive, and emotional signals to be integrated within the BF, the distinct projections by different cell types may enhance the versatility of the BF in coordinating diverse functions of multiple brain networks.
evidence: This is inferred from the divergent output patterns observed across cell types.

claim: The study targeted the caudal portion of the BF (including the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca, magnocellular preoptic nucleus, and substantia innominata) rather than the rostral nuclei.
source: For the current study, we targeted the caudal portion of the BF (including the horizontal limb of the diagonal band of Broca, magnocellular preoptic nucleus, and substantia innominata) rather than the rostral nuclei (medial septum and the vertical limb of the diagonal band of Broca).
evidence: This describes the specific anatomical targeting of the study.

claim: Very few non-specific labeling (<30 per brain) was found at >850 μm from the injection center in control experiments without RG.
source: To determine the spatial extent of the local contamination, we performed control experiments in the absence of RG and found very few non-specific labeling at >850 μm from the injection center (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments to assess technical limitations.

claim: Presynaptic neurons were counted only in coronal sections outside of the 850 μm exclusion zone.
source: Thus, presynaptic neurons were counted only in coronal sections outside of this range.
evidence: This describes the data analysis procedure to minimize contamination.

claim: When the brain was removed for histological processing, the olfactory bulb was often damaged, which led to a significant underestimation of labeling in the olfactory bulb.
source: Another technical limitation of the study is that when the brain was removed for histological processing, the olfactory bulb was often damaged, which led to a significant underestimation of labeling (both the input neurons and axon projections) in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the study.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of labeled neurons between the four cell types (P = 0.27, one-way ANOVA).
source: Since the number of labeled neurons varied across brain samples, and there was no significant difference between the four cell types (P = 0.27, one-way ANOVA), we normalized the data in each area by the total number of labeled neurons in each brain.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from comparing labeled neuron counts across cell types.

claim: The data in each area was normalized by the total number of labeled neurons in each brain.
source: Since the number of labeled neurons varied across brain samples, and there was no significant difference between the four cell types (P = 0.27, one-way ANOVA), we normalized the data in each area by the total number of labeled neurons in each brain.
evidence: This describes the data normalization procedure.

claim: The basolateral nucleus of the amygdala, immediately adjacent to the central nucleus, showed very sparse or no labeling.
source: Interestingly, many close neighbors of these densely labeled structures (e.g., the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala, immediately adjacent to the central nucleus) showed very sparse or no labeling, indicating high spatial specificity of the long-range inputs.
evidence: This observation demonstrates the spatial specificity of the input mapping.

claim: The long-range inputs to BF show high spatial specificity.
source: Interestingly, many close neighbors of these densely labeled structures (e.g., the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala, immediately adjacent to the central nucleus) showed very sparse or no labeling, indicating high spatial specificity of the long-range inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential labeling in adjacent brain structures.

claim: While several cell types projected strongly to the lateral habenula, few axons were detected in the immediately adjacent medial habenula.
source: For example, while several cell types projected strongly to the lateral habenula (Figure 5), few axons were detected in the immediately adjacent but anatomically distinct medial habenula (Hikosaka, 2010).
evidence: This observation demonstrates the spatial specificity of the output projections.

claim: The output projections from BF show high spatial specificity.
source: For example, while several cell types projected strongly to the lateral habenula (Figure 5), few axons were detected in the immediately adjacent but anatomically distinct medial habenula (Hikosaka, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential projections to adjacent brain structures.
